opus-5.5.text:
I think distillation is one of those ideas that's been around for a while (Geoff Hinton, Oriol Vinyals, and I wrote the original paper back in 2014 or so), but it's become much more important now that we have these really capable large models.

The basic insight is that a big model trained on a huge amount of data learns a lot of structure about the problem, and much of that is captured not just in its top answer but in the full distribution of its outputs. When you train a smaller model on the hard labels alone, you're throwing away a lot of information. If you instead train it to match the larger model's soft outputs, the small model gets a much richer signal per example. It learns which wrong answers are "almost right," how similar different things are, and so on. That lets you get much closer to the big model's quality with a fraction of the parameters and a lot less compute at inference time.

So the sweet spot is that you can do the expensive thing once. You train the very large, very capable model and push the frontier there, then distill it into smaller models that are cheap and fast enough to serve to huge numbers of people, or to run on a phone or in latency-sensitive settings. In practice, a distilled small model is often substantially better than the same-size model trained from scratch on the same data.

It also changes how you think about the whole family of models. You want the biggest, best model you can build, not necessarily to serve it everywhere, but because it becomes the teacher that raises the quality of everything below it. Each new generation's small, efficient models end up roughly as good as, or better than, the previous generation's large models, and distillation is a big part of why that keeps happening.

r001.rationale: It says hard-label training throws away information, while matching the large model’s soft outputs teaches the smaller model richer distinctions such as which wrong answers are almost right.

r002.rationale: It states that distillation lets a smaller model get “much closer” to the large model’s quality.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the core observation is that when you train a really large model, a lot of what it's learned is sort of latent in the full output distribution, not just in the single correct answer. When you train a small model from scratch on hard labels, you're throwing most of that away. You're telling it "the answer is cat," but you're not telling it that this image is a lot more like a dog than it is like a truck, or that this sentence could plausibly continue a few different ways with different probabilities. That dark knowledge, as Geoff Hinton called it, is actually a much richer training signal than the raw data.

So distillation lets you take a model that has effectively spent an enormous amount of compute figuring out the structure of the problem, and transfer a lot of that understanding into something that's much cheaper to serve. And it's a sweet spot for a few reasons. One is that the small model doesn't have to discover everything on its own. It's getting a smoothed, informative target on every example, so it tends to learn faster and generalize better than if it just saw the same data with hard labels. Two is that you can be very deliberate about it. You can generate exactly the kind of data you care about from the large model, including data for tasks or domains that are rare in the natural distribution, and then distill on that. And three, you often get to spend the big training compute once and then amortize it across a whole family of smaller models at different sizes for different deployment constraints, whether that's a phone, a browser, or a very high-volume serving path where latency and cost really matter.

I'd also say we've consistently seen that the gap between a distilled model and a model trained from scratch at the same size is pretty substantial. So if you've already made the investment in a large, high-quality model, distillation is one of the most compute-efficient ways to get a lot of that capability into something that's practical to run at scale. It's not magic, you still lose something going down in size, but you lose a lot less than you otherwise would.

r001.rationale: The response says hard labels discard information in the large model’s output distribution and that distillation gives the smaller model richer targets, helping it learn and generalize better than hard-label training alone.

r002.rationale: The response says distillation narrows the loss in capability when reducing model size, but does not say the smaller model can perform very close to the largest model.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal is that you can separate the cost of learning a capability from the cost of serving it. You can spend a lot of computation training a large model, and then use that model to provide a much richer training signal for a smaller one.

Instead of just saying, “Here’s the right answer,” the teacher can give you information about which alternatives are plausible, or generate examples that help the smaller model learn particular behaviors. That can be a more effective use of the smaller model’s capacity than training it on the original data alone.

You’re not going to squeeze every capability of a very large model into a tiny one. But if you care about a particular set of tasks, you can often retain a lot of the quality while substantially reducing inference cost and latency. And because you pay that inference cost every time someone uses the model, that’s a pretty attractive tradeoff.

r001.rationale: The response says a teacher can provide richer signals than right answers and help the smaller model learn particular behaviors, but it does not state that those behaviors would not emerge from hard-label training alone.

r002.rationale: It says a smaller model can retain “a lot” of the quality for selected tasks, but does not clearly say its performance can come very close to the largest model’s.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the appeal is that the model you use to produce training data doesn’t have to have the same constraints as the model you deploy. You can use a much larger model, spend more computation getting good answers, and then train a smaller model on those answers.

That gives the smaller model a much richer learning signal, especially if you can generate examples that cover the things you actually want it to do. You’re using the larger model’s capabilities to make the training process more effective, while keeping inference fast and inexpensive.

You shouldn’t expect the smaller model to inherit every capability of the larger one. But for a particular set of tasks, you can often get a very attractive tradeoff between quality, latency, and cost.

r001.rationale: The response says a larger model provides a richer learning signal, but does not state that distillation elicits behavior that hard-label training alone would not produce.

r002.rationale: It describes an attractive quality, latency, and cost tradeoff, but does not say the smaller model can perform very close to the largest model.
